comments.text:
The dead-code diagnostic on bds-yyz changes what this bead costs.

The machinery already exists and is fully written -- it is simply never
called. All of it is in the "referenced nowhere" bucket:

  src/error/structured.rs:989   levenshtein_distance
  src/error/structured.rs:1029  find_similar_ids
  src/error/structured.rs:347   StructuredError::issue_not_found
                                (which takes `existing_ids: &[String]`
                                precisely so it can suggest)

Also dead alongside them: ambiguous_id, cycle_detected, not_initialized,
invalid_priority, invalid_status, invalid_type, and the three *_HINT
constants they format.

So this is not "write a did-you-mean feature". It is "wire the constructor
that was written for it", and the same edit likely fixes the sibling error
messages too, since they went dark as a group -- which suggests one call site
stopped using StructuredError's constructors rather than seven separate
omissions. Worth finding that single point before writing anything new.

Caveat before trusting it: none of that code has ever run in production, so
it is unproven rather than merely unused. Check the suggestion threshold in
find_similar_ids against real IDs (bds-xxx are short, and Levenshtein over
short random suffixes suggests aggressively) before exposing it.

title: br completions -o never prints the install instructions it ships
description:
`src/cli/commands/completions.rs:94` holds `print_install_instructions`, sixty
lines of per-shell guidance covering bash, zsh (user, Oh My Zsh), fish,
PowerShell and elvish — where to put the file, what to add to the rc file, how
to reload the shell. It is never called. `rust-analyzer` `findReferences`
returns its definition and nothing else.

## Where it was clearly meant to go

`completions::execute` (`:31`) has two branches. The stdout branch is fine —
the user is piping, they know where it goes. The `-o` branch is the one with
the hole (`:35-45`):

```rust
if let Some(output_path) = &args.output {
    let mut file = std::fs::File::create(output_path)?;
    write_dynamic_completions(args.shell, &cmd, &mut file)?;
    info!(path = %output_path.display(), "Wrote completion script");
    eprintln!(
        "Generated {} completions to {}",
        shell_name(args.shell),
        output_path.display()
    );
}
```

A user who ran `br completions zsh -o ~/.zsh/completions/_br` is told a file was
written and nothing else. Whether it will be picked up depends on `fpath`, and
that is exactly what the unreachable function explains.

## Severity, honestly

Low. The user can find this in `docs/CLI_REFERENCE.md` or by reading the
module's own doc comment at `:1-16`, which shows the same paths. Nobody is
blocked. It is filed because the fix is a two-line change to a branch that
already exists, and because a sixty-line block of user-facing prose sitting
unreachable is the kind of thing that gets deleted by a future dead-code sweep
without anyone noticing it was meant to be shown.

## Decide which way to go

Both outcomes are defensible; pick one rather than leaving it:

- **Print it.** Call `print_install_instructions(args.shell)` after the
  `eprintln!` in the `-o` branch. Note it writes to stderr throughout, which is
  correct — it must not contaminate a redirected completion script — and note
  that `br completions zsh -o /dev/stdout` would then interleave, which is
  a pathological invocation but worth a moment's thought.
  Consider gating on `!ctx.is_quiet()`; `execute` currently ignores its
  `OutputContext` entirely (the parameter is `_ctx`), and `--quiet` suppressing
  the existing `eprintln!` too would be a small consistency win.
- **Delete it.** If `docs/CLI_REFERENCE.md` and the module doc comment are
  considered the canonical place for this, say so and remove the function.

## Acceptance criteria

- `br completions zsh -o <file>` either prints install guidance on stderr or the
  guidance is deleted — no third state where it exists unreachable.
- If printed: stdout is unaffected, so
  `br completions bash > file` still produces a byte-identical script to today.
- If printed: an e2e test asserts the guidance appears for `-o` and does not
  appear when writing to stdout.
- `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN task check` exits 0.
close_reason: print_install_instructions is now called from the -o branch, gated on !ctx.is_quiet() along with the existing 'Generated ...' line. Three e2e tests cover -o printing it, stdout not printing it, and --quiet suppressing it; the existing file_output_matches_stdout guard confirms stdout is unchanged. Also fixed --output's help text, which claimed 'directory'. db3b639

title: Two hand-maintained copies of the ID-resolution algorithm; only one ships
description:
`src/util/id.rs` carries the partial-ID resolution algorithm twice, in two
functions that differ only in whether their lookup callbacks return `bool` /
`Vec<String>` or `Result<bool>` / `Result<Vec<String>>`:

- `IdResolver::resolve` (`:697`) — infallible callbacks
- `IdResolver::resolve_fallible` (`:790`) — fallible callbacks

Line for line they are the same four steps: trim and reject empty, normalise and
try exact, prepend the default prefix when the input has no `-` and retry, then
substring-match the hash portion, retain by prefix, and branch on
`matches.len()` being 0 / 1 / many. About eighty lines each, kept in sync by
hand.

Only the fallible one ships.

## What reaches production

`src/cli/commands/mod.rs:112` calls `resolve_all_fallible`, which calls
`resolve_fallible`. That is the entire production path.

The infallible half is reachable only from:

- `resolve_all` (`:871`) — itself dead, `findReferences` returns its definition
  alone
- `resolve_id` (`:952`) — dead; re-exported from `src/util/mod.rs:21` but never
  called through that path either
- `resolve_id_fallible` (`:968`) — dead, despite the name; the live caller uses
  `resolve_all_fallible`
- the `#[cfg(test)]` module in the same file, from `:1007` onward

So `IdResolver::resolve` exists to be unit-tested and for nothing else.

## Why this is worth more than a delete

The tests that exercise the dead copy are testing real logic, and some of that
logic is subtle enough to deserve tests:

- Step 3 splits the normalised input with `split_prefix_remainder` and, when a
  prefix was present, retains only candidates starting with `{prefix}-`. Get
  that wrong and `bd-abc` resolves against `bds-abc`.
- `find_matching_ids` (`:914`) has hierarchical-child handling — a search for
  `64up6.4` must match `bds-64up6.4` rather than stripping the child suffix off
  the candidate — with a comment saying so, which reads like the residue of a
  fixed bug. `tests/repro/dotted_id_resolution.rs` exists.

Deleting the infallible copy and its tests would drop that coverage. Deleting
the copy and *porting* the tests onto `resolve_fallible` keeps it, at the cost
of wrapping each mock closure in `Ok(...)`. That is the version to do.

The risk of the status quo is the ordinary one for duplicated logic: a fix
lands in one copy. Because the tests point at the copy that does not ship, a
fix applied only to the dead one would still turn the suite green.

## Suggested fix

1. Port the `#[cfg(test)]` cases from the infallible resolver onto
   `resolve_fallible`, wrapping the mock callbacks in `Ok`.
2. Delete `IdResolver::resolve`, `resolve_all`, `resolve_id`,
   `resolve_id_fallible`, and drop `resolve_id` from the `src/util/mod.rs:21`
   re-export list.
3. Check `IdResolver::with_defaults` (`:664`) and `IdResolver::with_prefix`
   (`:670`) afterwards — both are currently reached only from the dead helpers
   and from tests, so after step 2 they may be test-only. If the tests are the
   only caller, that is fine, but say so rather than leaving it ambiguous.
   (Note there are two unrelated `with_prefix` / `with_defaults` pairs in this
   file — `ResolverConfig`'s at `:613` / `:46` and `IdGenerator`'s — so check
   which one a reference belongs to before removing anything.)

## Acceptance criteria

- One implementation of the resolution algorithm remains.
- Every behaviour previously asserted against the infallible copy is asserted
  against the surviving one — verified by diffing `cargo nextest list --workspace`
  before and after and accounting for each renamed or removed test by name.
- `tests/repro/dotted_id_resolution.rs` still passes.
- `src/util/mod.rs`'s re-export list contains no name that no longer exists.
- `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN task check` exits 0.
close_reason: Collapsed in 89c4510: resolve/resolve_all deleted, resolve_fallible/resolve_all_fallible are the single copy, tests repointed.

title: Remaining unreferenced pub items
description:
The unreferenced `pub` items left over once the larger clusters in this batch
are accounted for. Each was found by counting identifier occurrences across
`src/`, `tests/`, `test-support/` and `examples/` and keeping those that occur
exactly as often as they are defined; a sample was re-verified with
`rust-analyzer`'s `findReferences`, which agreed in every case checked.

Filed as one bead rather than fifteen because the individual judgements are
small and mostly identical. It is still a judgement per item — several of these
are worth keeping.

## Superseded config / storage entry points

Almost certainly delete: each has a strictly more capable successor already in
use.

| Location | Item | Successor |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `src/config/mod.rs:2320` | `open_storage` | `open_storage_with_cli` |
| `src/config/mod.rs:3464` | `load_startup_config` | `load_startup_config_with_paths` |
| `src/config/mod.rs:216` | `ConfigPaths::legacy_user_config_path` | `load_legacy_user_config` reads the path directly |
| `src/cli/mod.rs:1276` | `resolve_output_format_basic` | the non-`_basic` resolver |

## Storage query methods with no caller

| Location | Item |
| --- | --- |
| `src/storage/sqlite.rs:2123` | `status_revision` |
| `:10244` | `count_dependencies_for_issues` |
| `:10294` | `get_blocking_dependents_for_issue_ids` |
| `:10510` | `count_dependents_for_issues` |
| `:6481` | `get_blocks_dep_edges_for_issue_ids` |
| `:11023` | `get_issues_needing_export` |
| `:11109` | `delete_metadata` |
| `:12936` | `clear_all_dirty_flags` |
| `:12946` | `count_exportable_issues` |
| `:1955` | `get_all_events` (see below) |

Three of these deserve a second look before deletion rather than a reflex:

- `get_blocking_dependents_for_issue_ids` (`:10294`) and
  `get_blocks_dep_edges_for_issue_ids` (`:6481`) are the *bounded* variants of
  edge lookups whose unbounded siblings are live. Their doc comments say the
  point is to keep focused traversals from hydrating the whole workspace graph,
  and both handle the SQLite parameter limit by falling back to a full scan.
  If a live caller is currently using the unbounded form on a small id set,
  the right fix is to switch it over, not to delete the bounded one.
- `get_issues_needing_export` (`:11023`) implements incremental export —
  filtering dirty issues whose content hash matches the stored export hash. The
  incremental auto-flush path in `src/sync/mod.rs` may want exactly this;
  check `collect_incremental_auto_flush_changes` (`sync/mod.rs:3390`) before
  discarding.
- `clear_all_dirty_flags` (`:12936`) and `delete_metadata` (`:11109`) look like
  recovery/repair primitives. If a `br doctor --repair` path is planned, they
  belong to it.

### The wrapper-pair blind spot

`SqliteStorage::get_all_events` (`sqlite.rs:1955`) has no callers, and it is the
*only* caller of `events::get_all_events` (`events.rs:456`). Both are dead, but
an occurrence-counting sweep cannot see it: the wrapper and the inner function
share a name, so each inflates the other's count. Same shape for
`events::count_events` (`events.rs:481`), whose one reference is inside that
file's own test module.

These two are the reason the sibling bead about the missing dead-code gate asks
for a tool that resolves references properly rather than counting identifiers.
They overlap with the dead event-writer bead; whichever lands first should take
them.

## Small predicates and accessors

Delete-on-sight unless a caller is imminent:

| Location | Item |
| --- | --- |
| `src/error/mod.rs:267` | `suggests_force` |
| `src/health.rs:38` | `WorkspaceHealth::is_fatal` |
| `src/model/mod.rs:125` | `is_draft` |
| `src/model/mod.rs:245` | `is_standard` |
| `src/output/context.rs:551` | `error_panel` |
| `src/storage/conn.rs:520` | `SqliteValue::as_float` |
| `src/storage/conn.rs:530` | `SqliteValue::as_blob` |
| `src/validation/mod.rs:563` | `assert_no_git_in_sync` |

Two notes:

- `WorkspaceHealth::is_fatal` is the odd one out of a set: `is_operable` and
  `needs_recovery` on the same enum are live. An `Unsafe` workspace is
  presumably meant to be refused somewhere; worth one grep of the health
  consumers to confirm the `Unsafe` case is handled by other means before
  removing the predicate that names it.
- `as_float` / `as_blob` round out `SqliteValue`'s accessor set alongside the
  live `as_text` / `as_integer`. Keeping an accessor family complete is a
  legitimate reason to retain them; if so, that is a comment, not silence.

## `test-support`

`test-support/src/` has several files carrying a blanket `#![allow(dead_code)]`
(`assertions.rs:1`, `binary_discovery.rs:6`, `dataset_registry.rs:6`,
`fixtures.rs:1`, `ordering.rs:13`), which suppresses the lint for genuinely
private items too. Behind it: `assert_issue_exists`, `assert_status`,
`print_table`, `available_datasets`, `init_git`, `read_file`, `list_dir`,
`slowest_command`, `allow_either`, `push_step`, `thorough`, `with_iterations`,
`with_bd`, `measure_io_sizes`, `compute_statistics`, `with_normalization`.

Lowest priority in this bead, and arguably correct as-is — a shared test harness
reasonably keeps a wider surface than any one test uses. But `with_bd` in
particular names something that no longer exists in this fork, and the blanket
allow means nobody will ever be told. Worth one pass narrowing the allows to the
items that actually need them.

## Acceptance criteria

- Every item above is deleted, or retained with an `#[allow(dead_code)]` and a
  comment saying why and what will consume it.
- The three storage methods flagged for a second look have an explicit decision
  recorded, not a default one.
- `test-support`'s blanket `#![allow(dead_code)]` attributes are either narrowed
  or justified in a comment.
- `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN task check` exits 0, and `cargo test --test licensing`
  passes after staging.
notes:
Second sweep (2026-08-02). Unreachable-from-main spans: 128 -> 29.

Removed this pass: the export preflight (a second implementation of two rules
export_to_jsonl already enforces); the duplicated export traversal, so the
ExportErrorPolicy tests now drive the loop that ships; --orphans, a CLI flag
the import engine never consulted; the inert `actor` argument threaded through
mutate() into eleven storage methods; IssuePanel's unreachable no-details

title: rust-version contradicts its own bisection comment and CLAUDE.md
description:
`Cargo.toml:29` declares `rust-version = "1.97.1"`. The twenty-five line comment
immediately above it — a documented `cargo build --locked` bisection, toolchain
by toolchain — concludes:

> So 1.95 is the floor, and it is a floor someone has actually built with rather
> than a number nobody has tested.

and its table records `1.95.0 ok` / `1.96.0 ok`, with the failures at 1.88,
1.91, 1.93 and 1.94. `CLAUDE.md`'s "Toolchain floor" section states the same
thing a third way: *"`rust-version = "1.95"` in `Cargo.toml` is measured (by
bisection against this crate's dependency graph), not inherited from upstream."*

Three places, two answers.

## Why it matters here specifically

The comment is not decoration. It exists because the *previous* value was wrong
in exactly this way — inherited rather than measured, `1.88` carried over and
never tested, "wrong by seven releases" in the comment's own words. The whole
point of writing the bisection down was so the number could not drift away from
its evidence again. It has.

And nothing will catch it:

- `task toolchain:check` reads `rustc -vV` and fails only on nightly, beta or
  dev channels. It never compares the active toolchain against the manifest
  floor, so a stable toolchain below `rust-version` is not what it looks for.
  (Cargo itself will refuse to build in that case, so the practical failure is
  loud — but that is cargo, not the gate, and it says nothing about the value
  being *too high*.)
- Nothing at all catches a floor that is too high. `1.97.1` simply excludes
  users on 1.95 and 1.96 from a build the bisection says works.
- `tests/licensing.rs` sweeps tracked files but pins licence facts, not this.

The failure mode is silent exclusion: a contributor or packager on 1.96 gets
`package requires rustc 1.97.1 or newer` for a build that would have succeeded.

## Which value is right is an open question

Do not assume the comment. Two plausible stories:

- **The comment is stale.** Something in `Cargo.lock` moved its own requirement
  after the bisection was written — which is the exact scenario the comment
  itself anticipates: *"A future `libsqlite3-sys` may move it again, in either
  direction, with no change here."* If so, `1.97.1` is correct and the comment
  and `CLAUDE.md` need updating with a fresh bisection table.
- **The value is stale.** Someone bumped it to match a local toolchain. If so,
  it should go back to `1.95`.

Resolve it by measuring, not by picking. The comment documents the method:
install each toolchain and run `cargo build --locked` and
`cargo build --locked --all-targets`.

Also note the format: `rust-version` elsewhere in the file and in `CLAUDE.md` is
two-component (`1.95`). `1.97.1` is three. Cargo accepts both, but a patch-level
floor asserts something the bisection cannot support — the granularity of the
evidence is a minor release. Prefer `1.97` over `1.97.1` if the higher value
survives.

## Fix

1. Bisect against the current `Cargo.lock` and record the result.
2. Set `rust-version` to what was measured.
3. Update the comment's table and its concluding sentence to match.
4. Update `CLAUDE.md`'s "Toolchain floor" section.
5. Consider extending `task toolchain:check` to also compare `rustc -vV`'s
   release against the manifest's `rust-version`, so the two can at least be
   observed to disagree. That does not catch a floor set too high, which is the
   present bug — for that, the only real defence is that the comment, the
   manifest and `CLAUDE.md` are checked against each other, and that is worth
   considering as a small test since all three are tracked files.

## Acceptance criteria

- `Cargo.toml`'s `rust-version`, the bisection comment above it, and
  `CLAUDE.md`'s "Toolchain floor" section all state the same value.
- That value is backed by a `cargo build --locked` run on the toolchain named,
  and by a failing run one minor release below it, both recorded in the comment.
- `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN task check` exits 0 on the declared floor.
- `cargo test --test licensing` passes after staging (both `Cargo.toml` and
  `CLAUDE.md` are tracked and swept).
close_reason: Resolved against maintainer intent rather than by lowering the key: 1.97.1 is a deliberate support floor, not drift. The ticket assumed the three sources must state one value; they in fact carry two distinct facts (declared floor 1.97.1, measured minimum 1.95), and the contradiction was that the prose conflated them. Re-bisected against the current lock (1.94 fails on cfg_select, 1.95/1.96 build clean, needs --ignore-rust-version). Cargo.toml comment and CLAUDE.md rewritten to state both; tests/toolchain_floor.rs enforces agreement and floor >= minimum. 750fe83

title: Stale comment at the head of the 3-way merge decision table
description:
`merge_issue` (`src/sync/mod.rs:4845`) resolves a 3-way merge by matching on
`(base, left, right)`. The eight arms are labelled "Case 1" through "Case 8" and
the labels are what a reader navigates by. Case 1 is mislabelled:

```rust
// Case 1: Only in base (deleted in both local and external) -> no action
(Some(_), None, None) => MergeResult::Delete,
```

The parenthetical is right — present in base, gone from both sides, so both
agreed to delete it. The verdict is wrong: the comment says "no action", the
code returns `Delete`, and `Delete` is correct. `MergeResult::NoAction` is a
different variant, used at Case 8 (`:4997`) for the `(None, None, None)`
combination that cannot occur in practice.

`three_way_merge` treats them very differently — `Delete` pushes onto
`report.deleted` (`:5063`), `NoAction` does nothing (`:5055`) — so a reader who
trusts the comment concludes that a both-sides deletion is dropped on the floor
rather than propagated. This is the first arm of the table, i.e. the one
skim-read most often.

## Severity

Cosmetic. No behaviour is wrong and no test is affected. Filed because it sits
at the head of the merge decision table, because merge semantics are where
readers most need to trust the annotations, and because it costs one line.

## While in there

Two other things in the same match worth a glance, neither a defect:

- Case 6 (`:4927`) writes `(false | true, false) => ...`, which is just
  `(_, false)`. The comment above it explains the intent ("Neither changed OR
  only left changed"), and the verbose form arguably documents the two cases —
  but the `(false, false)` half is unreachable anyway, because the
  `l.sync_equals(r)` early return at `:4920` has already handled it. A short
  comment saying so would save the next reader the derivation.
- `MergeResult::NoAction` is reachable only from Case 8, which the code itself
  calls "impossible in practice". Leaving it is fine — `all_issue_ids` unions
  the three maps so the arm genuinely cannot fire, and an unreachable-but-total
  match is better than a `_ => unreachable!()`. Worth a word in the variant's
  doc comment that it exists for totality.

## Acceptance criteria

- The Case 1 comment states that the issue is deleted.
- `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN task check` exits 0.
close_reason: Case 1 comment now says 'delete', matching the arm's MergeResult::Delete. Also documented why Case 6's (false, false) half is unreachable and why NoAction exists for totality. a676258

title: source_repo_path publishes a local absolute path in every tracked issue
description:
`br create` stamps `source_repo_path` — the absolute canonical path of the
workspace — onto every new issue, and `Issue` serialises it straight into
`.beads/issues.jsonl`, which is a tracked file. Every issue this project has
ever filed therefore publishes the maintainer's home-directory layout to a
public GitHub repository.

Evidence, current working tree:

    $ python3 -c "import json;print({json.loads(l)['source_repo_path'] for l in open('.beads/issues.jsonl') if l.strip()})"
    {'<HOME>/Development/beads'}

All 29 records carry it. `source_repo` alongside it is just `beads` — the
basename — and is harmless.

Three things make this worth fixing rather than tolerating:

1. It is a leak with no consumer. Nothing reads the field to do anything.
   Grepping `src/` for non-construction uses finds only storage plumbing
   (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE column lists, the v10 migration, the update-mask
   struct) plus one comparison in `Issue::sync_equals`. No command filters on
   it, no output formats it, nothing routes on it. It is written, persisted,
   round-tripped, and never consulted.

2. It actively causes JSONL churn. `sync_equals` (src/model/mod.rs:706)
   compares `source_repo_path`, so the same issue synced from two clones of
   this repo at different paths — a second worktree, a CI checkout, a
   colleague's machine — is "changed" on every sync. That is a spurious diff
   and a merge conflict on a file whose whole point is to merge cleanly.

3. The project's own guard cannot see it. `tests/licensing.rs` exists to keep
   "a path onto someone else's machine" out of tracked files, but it
   enumerates via `git ls-files` and excludes `.beads/` by design (see the
   comment at tests/licensing.rs:43). So the one check written for this class
   of problem skips the one file that has it.

The test suite already treats the field as non-deterministic: 
tests/output_contracts.rs:581 collapses both `source_repo` and
`source_repo_path` to a `SOURCE_REPO` token because otherwise the snapshots
capture a random tempdir path.

The stated justification (`src/model/mod.rs:543`, upstream beads#289) is that
fleet automation needs to disambiguate two clones of one repo on the same
machine. That may hold for a fleet operator running many checkouts locally, but
it is paid for by every ordinary user, in a file they commit and push.
close_reason: Fixed: br create and the markdown import no longer derive source_repo_path from the workspace. canonical_source_repo_path() and the CreateConfig field are gone; source_repo (the basename) is unchanged. br update --source-repo-path still sets it explicitly and it round-trips. No schema migration — the nullable column and the v10 migration stand. Eight output-contract snapshots lost the key. The 31 tracked records were stripped and the local SQLite cleared to match. Regression coverage: tests/repro/source_repo_path_leak.rs.

title: Re-derive the bv contracts: the viewer is now a read-only JSONL consumer
description:
Every `bv`-shaped contract in this repository was written against the upstream
viewer (v0.18.0) — an interactive tool with `--robot-*` modes that emits `br`
commands for an operator to run. The viewer now in use is a different program:
<https://github.com/Toshik1978/beads-viewer>, a Go TUI that reads
`.beads/issues.jsonl`, renders it, and does nothing else. Its own README states
it never writes inside `.beads/` and never spawns a subprocess.

**The bv contract has never been enforced on CI.** `bv_robot_modes_emit_br_
commands_that_br_accepts` is the only test that touches the viewer, and
`bv_available_or_skip` returns false whenever no `bv` is on PATH. No CI job
installs one — ci.yml's three `taiki-e/install-action` steps fetch cargo-audit,
cargo-nextest and cargo-llvm-cov, and nothing else — so on every runner the
test announces a skip and passes. The contract is live only on a machine that
happens to have upstream bv installed, in practice a maintainer's.

That reframes the work. This is not a load-bearing guard that needs careful
migration; it is a check that has been nominal for its whole life in this repo
and is now also wrong. It fails safe today and will fail loudly later: install
the new viewer locally and the test stops skipping, because `--robot-next` is
not a mode it has, `run_bv` asserts on the non-zero exit, and the suite goes
red with something that reads like a `br` regression.

What remains of the robot machinery, precisely:

- `robot` appears **nowhere in `src/`**. The `--robot` flag was removed in
  e84fdd9 ("feat(cli)!: remove the --robot flag, leaving --json"), so the file
  name `robot_output.rs` and the snapshot name `robot_ready_output` are
  vestigial. The golden actually runs `br ready --json`.
- `tests/output_contracts/robot_output.rs` holds exactly two tests:
  `robot_golden_ready_output`, which is pure `br` and involves no viewer at
  all, and the bv interface test above.
- The file header records that three goldens of bv's *own* output once existed
  and were deleted under bds-04l.11 because they pinned v0.18.0's emoji strings
  and hint wording — roughly ninety lines of masking regex absorbing a
  downstream binary's drift. The interface test is what replaced them. Its
  premise expires with the new viewer, which emits no commands at all;
  grepping that repository for "robot" returns nothing.

So the surviving br-side robot contract is `robot_golden_ready_output` — the
shape of `br ready --json` — and that is worth keeping on its own merits,
independent of who reads it.

Full inventory of the remaining sites, so the review is bounded:

1. `tests/output_contracts/robot_output.rs` — the bv half: `BvRun`, `run_bv`,
   `bv_is_on_path`, `bv_available_or_skip`, `clear_inherited_br_env` (whose
   only caller is `run_bv`, line 147), `br_commands_in`, and the contract test.
   `init_robot_golden_workspace` and `assert_valid_json` must stay —
   `robot_golden_ready_output` uses both.

2. `src/cli/commands/init.rs:63-64` — the generated `.gitignore` ignores
   `/.bv.lock`. The new viewer writes no lock file, and its TUI state
   deliberately lives outside `.beads/`.

3. `src/cli/commands/init.rs:259` and `:367` — `br init` writes an empty
   `issues.jsonl`, commented as being "for compatibility with bv, an external
   consumer that expects this file to exist". The new viewer treats a missing
   file as an empty snapshot rather than an error, so that rationale is gone.
   Whether the file is still worth creating for `br`'s own reasons is a
   separate question — decide it, do not inherit it.

4. `NOTICE.md:56` — "The `.beads/` on-disk layout and the `issues.jsonl` schema
   are deliberately unchanged, so that [upstream viewer] keeps working." This
   names the upstream project, is one of only two files allowed to, and is a
   goal statement rather than a licence clause. It needs care but it is now
   inaccurate: the layout is being kept for a different consumer.

5. `src/storage/schema.rs:1541` and `src/sync/mod.rs:3929` — comments
   justifying status normalisation partly by "downstream consumers (bv,
   bd-style readers) reject unknown statuses". The normalisation is almost
   certainly still right for `br`'s own reasons; the justification should stop
   leaning on a binary nobody here controls.

6. `Taskfile.yml:118` — the `test:linux` note that `bv` is deliberately not
   installed in the container because the tests skip loudly. Dies with item 1.

What the new viewer actually decodes from each JSONL record, which is the only
real remaining coupling: id, title, description, design, acceptance_criteria,
notes, status, priority, issue_type, assignee, owner, estimated_minutes,
created_at, created_by, updated_at, closed_at, close_reason, due_at,
defer_until, external_ref, source_repo, deleted_at, pinned, ephemeral,
is_template, labels, dependencies, comments (id, author, text, created_at).

Note what is absent from that list: `source_repo_path` (see bds-31i) and
anything robot-shaped.
design:
The stated intent is that `br` stops carrying contracts on the viewer's behalf.
Taking that at face value gives a default disposition per site, with one that
genuinely needs a decision rather than an edit.

**Delete outright.**

- `tests/output_contracts/robot_output.rs`: the whole `bv` half — `BvRun`,
  `run_bv`, `bv_is_on_path`, `bv_available_or_skip`, `clear_inherited_br_env`
  (only caller is `run_bv`), `br_commands_in`, and
  `bv_robot_modes_emit_br_commands_that_br_accepts`. Keep
  `init_robot_golden_workspace`, `assert_valid_json` and
  `robot_golden_ready_output` — that golden is pure `br` and is the surviving
  robot-side contract. The file's own header (bds-04l.11) explains why the
  *rendering* goldens went and this interface test stayed; that reasoning
  expires with the interface. Nothing is lost from CI coverage by the deletion,
  because CI never ran it.

  Worth doing in the same pass: `robot` no longer appears in `src/` at all, so

title: sync --import-only silently ignores fields removed from the JSONL
description:
A field removed from a record in `.beads/issues.jsonl` is not removed from the
database. The old value survives the import, and the next write to that issue
exports it straight back into the JSONL — so a hand edit that deletes a field
appears to work, then silently undoes itself.

Measured, `br` 1.1.0, on a throwaway workspace each time:

    br create "probe"; br update <id> --assignee alice
    # remove "assignee" from the record in .beads/issues.jsonl
    br sync --import-only
      Imported from JSONL:
        Updated: 0 issues
        Skipped: 1 issues (up-to-date)
    sqlite3 .beads/beads.db 'select assignee from issues'  ->  alice

Not specific to one column. The same holds for `assignee`, `owner`,
`external_ref`, `design` and `source_repo_path` — every optional field tried.
The import reports the record as "up-to-date" while the two sides plainly
disagree, which is the part that makes it a bug rather than a policy: whatever
the intended semantics, "up-to-date" is the wrong word for "I ignored your
edit".

This is how it surfaced. Clearing `source_repo_path` from this repository's own
tracker (bds-31i) could not be done by stripping the JSONL and re-importing,
which is what that ticket's acceptance criteria assumed. The database kept all
31 values, and the first subsequent `br update` on any issue would have written
its path back into the committed file. The fix had to clear the SQLite column
directly.

A second, separate short-circuit sits in front of this one: when the JSONL's
whole-file hash is unchanged since the last import, `br sync --import-only`
prints "JSONL is current (hash unchanged since last import)" and does no
per-record work at all. That is reasonable on its own, but it means two
successive edits that produce the same file content behave differently
depending on import history — worth confirming it does what is intended once
the per-record semantics are settled.

Note that `content_hash` is not the mechanism. Exported records do not carry
the field at all — a fresh record's keys are exactly id, title, status,
priority, issue_type, created_at, created_by, updated_at, source_repo,
assignee, compaction_level, original_size — so the per-record "up-to-date"
verdict is computed from a comparison, not read from the file.

title: Delete the events subsystem wholesale
description:
Events cost a write on every mutation and a schema, a storage module and roughly 400 lines of tests, and nothing reads them except one opt-in close-policy gate. Decision taken 2026-08-01: delete the whole subsystem rather than keep or make it durable.

## What events actually did

Intended role, inherited from the Go original: a per-mutation audit log, deliberately DB-only and never exported to JSONL so the sync round-trip is unaffected.

Actual role in this tree, measured:

- br close -> close.rs:140 -> SqliteStorage::find_last_in_progress_actor -> reads status_changed events -> enforces close_policy.forbid_self_close_after_in_progress. That gate defaults to off and is set in no config observed.
- Nothing else. IssueDetails.events exists but br show passes include_events: false (show.rs:464), so it is always empty and skip_serializing_if keeps it out of --json entirely. Only tests pass true.
- count_events, get_all_events (both the storage::events fn and its SqliteStorage wrapper) have no callers at all.

## Why deleting beats keeping

Events never reach issues.jsonl -- Issue has no events field -- and .beads/*.db is gitignored and derived, with the JSONL as the source of truth. So the log does not travel between clones and any DB rebuild erases it. The one gate it powers therefore degrades silently: no in_progress event found, find_last_in_progress_actor returns None, no violation, close allowed. An audit trail a routine rebuild erases is not one.

## Scope

Delete: src/storage/events.rs; the events table DDL, indexes and column backfill in schema.rs; MutationContext::record_event / record_field_change and the ten-column INSERT in sqlite.rs; every ctx.record_* call site; get_events / get_all_events / count_events / find_last_in_progress_actor; the include_events parameter and IssueDetails.events; EventType and Event in model/mod.rs; the forbid_self_close_after_in_progress gate, its evaluate_self_close evaluator and its config-key registry entry.

Decisions taken with the scope:

- Config key: hard removal. close_policy structs use serde(deny_unknown_fields), so a config.yaml setting the key will fail to parse with an unknown-field error naming it. Accepted deliberately over a deprecation shim; the gate defaults to off and nothing observed sets it.
- Table: dropped by migration, bumping CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION 16 -> 17, rather than left vestigial.

## Supersedes

bds-dhr and bds-ip3 both become moot -- the dead writer layer and the duplicate events DDL are deleted along with everything else. Close them against this rather than doing them first.

Note bds-dhr is wrong on one point and it should not be carried forward: it claims EventType::Updated and EventType::DependencyRemoved are unreachable and asks for a decision on whether to emit them. Both are emitted in production today (sqlite.rs:3572, :9395 and :8550, :8610, :8661, :8769); the sites it checked were the dead wrappers, not the live inline path.

## Acceptance criteria

- No table named events in a freshly initialised database, and an existing v16 database is migrated without error.
- grep for EventType, storage::events and record_event over src/ returns nothing.
- br info --schema no longer publishes Event or EventType, and the output-contract snapshots are regenerated deliberately.
- br show --json output is byte-identical to before (the field was always omitted).
- Test names are diffed with cargo nextest list --workspace before and after and every removal is explained, not reconciled by arithmetic.
- env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN task check exits 0 and cargo test --test licensing passes after staging.

title: Intent-detection hints are shadowed by the static suggestion
description:
`StructuredError::generate_hint` computes intent-detection hints for
`--priority`, `--status` and `--type` that no user can ever see. Its first
statement short-circuits on the error's own static suggestion:

```rust
fn generate_hint(err: &BeadsError, context: Option<&Value>) -> Option<String> {
    if let Some(suggestion) = err.suggestion() {
        return Some(suggestion.to_string());
    }
    match err {
        BeadsError::InvalidPriority { priority } => { ...detect_priority_intent... }
        BeadsError::InvalidStatus { status } => { ...detect_status_intent... }
        BeadsError::InvalidType { issue_type } => { ...detect_type_intent... }
```

`BeadsError::suggestion()` (src/error/mod.rs:277) returns `Some(...)` for all
three variants, so the `match` arms below are unreachable for exactly the
variants they were written for.

## What the user gets instead

    $ br create x --priority high
    Hint: Use a priority between 0 (critical) and 4 (backlog)

rather than the "Did you mean --priority 1?" the dead arm would have produced.
The static text is not wrong, just markedly less useful: `detect_priority_intent`
already resolved "high" to 1 and the answer is discarded.

## It is not entirely lost

`extract_code_and_context` calls the same detectors and puts the result in the
machine-readable context, so `--json` consumers see:

    "context": { "status": "done", "hint": "Did you mean --status closed?" }

while the top-level `hint` field carries only the static list. So the JSON
surface has the good hint in the wrong field, and the human surface does not
have it at all.

## Why it is filed separately

Found while wiring bds-k7e, which is the same defect one level up: machinery
written, never reached. The fix is not obviously "delete the short-circuit" --
`suggestion()` is the right answer for the dozen variants that have no
detector, and the ordering was presumably meant to be a fallback rather than a
pre-emption. Likeliest shape: consult the specific arms first and fall back to
`suggestion()`, which inverts the current precedence.

Worth checking whether any test pins the current wording before changing it;
`invalid_priority_error_is_retryable_and_explains_the_range` in
src/error/structured.rs deliberately asserts the static text and carries a
comment pointing here.

## Acceptance criteria

- `br create x --priority high` hints at `--priority 1`.
- The variants with no detector keep their `suggestion()` text unchanged.
- The `--json` context keeps its `hint` key, or the duplication is removed
  deliberately and documented in docs/CLI_REFERENCE.md.
- `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN task check` exits 0.

title: Multi-key --sort for br list and br search
description:
Replace the single `--sort` key on `br list`/`br search` with a comma-separated spec (`--sort priority,updated`), parsed once into a shared `SortSpec` value that both the SQL ORDER BY builder and the in-memory comparator consume. Adds `status`, `type` and `assignee` to the sort vocabulary, since low-cardinality keys are the ones that make a secondary key meaningful.

Architecture: a new `src/model/sort.rs` owns `SortField`/`SortDirection`/`SortKey`/`SortSpec` with `FromStr` plus two renderers (`order_by_sql`, `cmp`) and one predicate (`as_single_field`). `ListFilters.sort` becomes `Option<SortSpec>`, moving parsing and validation to the CLI boundary and deleting the two duplicate `validate_sort_key` functions and the two near-identical ORDER BY blocks.

Tech stack: Rust, rusqlite (bundled SQLite), clap, proptest, insta, cargo-nextest.
design:
# Multi-key `--sort` for `br list` and `br search`

## Goal

`--sort` accepts one key. The keys worth combining are the low-cardinality
ones — `priority`, `status`, `type`, `assignee` — because they are the only
keys that produce enough ties for a second key to break. None of them can
currently be a primary key with a chosen tiebreaker, so the ordering people
actually want each morning ("highest priority first, most recently touched
first within each band") is unreachable.

This replaces the single sort key with a comma-separated spec, parsed once
into a shared `SortSpec` value that both the SQL builder and the in-memory
comparator consume.

## Why a shared value rather than a wider match

Today the sort key is an unparsed `Option<String>` re-interpreted
independently in five places:

| Site | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `src/cli/mod.rs:145` | `SORT_KEY_CANDIDATES`, shell completion |
| `src/cli/commands/list.rs:627` | `validate_sort_key` |
| `src/cli/commands/search.rs:501` | `validate_sort_key`, a duplicate of the above |
| `src/storage/sqlite.rs:4053` | `ORDER BY` builder for `list_issues` |
| `src/storage/sqlite.rs:4811` | `ORDER BY` builder for search, a near-copy |
| `src/cli/commands/search.rs:618` | `apply_sort_by_issue`, the in-memory sort |

`br list` sorts in SQL on some paths and re-sorts in Rust after
`apply_client_filters` on others (`requires_post_query_ordering`). Those two
orderings must agree, and today they are independently hand-written — which
is precisely how they would drift apart without anything failing. Widening
each `match` arm to handle N keys would multiply that hazard by the number of
new fields. One parsed spec with two renderers, plus a property test
asserting the renderers agree, makes the drift impossible rather than
unlikely.

## Grammar

```
--sort <key>[,<key>...]

key   := ['-' | '+'] field
field := priority | status | type | assignee
       | created_at | updated_at | title
```

Aliases: `created` -> `created_at`, `updated` -> `updated_at`.

### Direction

A bare field takes its **natural** direction, which is the direction that
field already has as a single key today:

| Field | Bare direction | Reading |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `priority` | ASC | critical first (priority 0 is critical) |
| `status` | ASC | open first, in workflow order |
| `type` | ASC | declaration order |
| `assignee` | ASC | A-Z, unassigned last |
| `title` | ASC | A-Z |
| `created_at` | DESC | newest first |
| `updated_at` | DESC | newest first |

`-` forces descending, `+` forces ascending. `--reverse` flips every key in
the resolved spec, so it keeps composing with whatever was written.

Every spec is terminated by an implicit `id ASC`, so output is always
deterministic. `--reverse` does not flip that terminator.

Resolution is a single named step — natural directions applied, the legacy
carve-out expanded, `--reverse` folded in, `id ASC` appended — producing a
flat `Vec<SortKey>`. Both renderers and the index fast-path guard consume
that one output, so no consumer re-derives any part of it.

### Errors

Rejected at the CLI boundary, before any query runs:

- an unknown field name
- a duplicate field within one spec (`priority,-priority`)
- an empty segment (`priority,,title`, a leading or trailing comma)
- an empty spec (`--sort ''`)

### The one legacy carve-out

A spec consisting of a single bare `priority` expands to
`priority ASC, created_at DESC, id ASC`, preserving today's output exactly.
Any explicit direction, or any second key, makes the spec literal.

`--reverse` flips the carve-out's inherited `created_at` key along with the
`priority` key, so `--sort priority --reverse` stays
`priority DESC, created_at ASC, id ASC` exactly as it is today
(`sqlite.rs:4055`).

`--sort priority,created` spells the legacy behaviour explicitly and is the
migration path for anyone who wants it alongside other keys.

The no-`--sort` default is unchanged: `priority ASC, created_at DESC, id ASC`.

## Field semantics

### Enum ordering

`Status` and `IssueType` derive only `PartialEq, Eq, Hash` — no `Ord` — so
the ordering is explicit. Each gains one `sort_rank()` method in
`src/model/mod.rs` following declaration order. That single table is rendered
two ways, as a `CASE` expression in SQL and read directly by the Rust
comparator, so the engines cannot disagree about what "status order" means.

| Field | Order |
| --- | --- |
| `status` | open, in_progress, blocked, deferred, draft, closed, tombstone, pinned, then custom |
| `type` | task, bug, feature, epic, chore, docs, question, then custom |

Both enums have a `Custom(String)` variant. All custom values share the last
rank and break ties alphabetically among themselves:

```sql
ORDER BY CASE status WHEN 'open' THEN 0 ... ELSE 99 END <dir>, status <dir>
```

The trailing `status` key only ever fires inside the custom bucket, because
every known status has a distinct rank, so it cannot perturb the documented
order of known statuses.

### Assignee and NULL

`assignee` folds `NULL` and `''` together via `NULLIF(assignee,'')`, matching
the existing unassigned convention at `sqlite.rs:4012`, `:4533`, `:4768` and
`:5247` (`assignee IS NULL OR assignee = ''`).

Unassigned sorts **last in both directions**: `--sort -assignee` should
reverse the names, not dredge the nameless to the top. Both engines need an
explicit correction for this, since SQLite puts NULL first in ASC and Rust's
`Option` ordering puts `None` first:

```sql
CASE WHEN NULLIF(assignee,'') IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END ASC, assignee <dir>
```

The null-rank key is always ASC regardless of the key's direction.

### Text and numbers

`title` keeps `COLLATE NOCASE` in SQL and `to_lowercase()` in Rust, as today.
`priority` is an INTEGER column where 0 is critical, so ascending is
critical-first and no mapping is needed. `created_at` and `updated_at` are
RFC3339 DATETIME columns that sort correctly as text.

## Components

### `src/model/sort.rs` (new)

```rust
pub enum SortField { Priority, Status, Type, Assignee, CreatedAt, UpdatedAt, Title }
pub enum SortDirection { Asc, Desc }
pub struct SortKey { field: SortField, direction: SortDirection }
pub struct SortSpec(Vec<SortKey>);
```

`SortSpec` implements `FromStr` (parsing, alias resolution, direction
defaulting, duplicate and empty-segment rejection) and exposes one resolution
step feeding two renderers:

- `resolved(&self, reverse: bool) -> Vec<SortKey>` — applies natural
  directions, expands the legacy carve-out, folds in `--reverse`, and appends
  the `id ASC` terminator. The single source of the effective ordering.
- `order_by_sql(&self, reverse: bool) -> String` — renders `resolved()` as a
  SQL `ORDER BY` clause, for both SQL builders.
- `cmp(&self, a: &Issue, b: &Issue, reverse: bool) -> Ordering` — walks
  `resolved()`, for the in-memory path.

The index fast-path guard consumes `resolved()` directly rather than
inspecting the unparsed spec, so it cannot disagree with what the renderers
actually emit.

`SortField` owns its natural direction, its SQL column expression, and its
Rust key extraction. Adding a field means touching one enum and its three
`match` arms, not five call sites.

### `ListFilters`

`sort: Option<String>` becomes `Option<SortSpec>` (`sqlite.rs:10151`).
`ListFilters` derives only `Debug, Clone, Default` — no serde — so the type
change is safe. Parsing and validation move to the CLI boundary in
`build_filters`, which deletes both duplicate `validate_sort_key` functions.

## Call sites

| File | Change |
| --- | --- |
| `src/cli/mod.rs:145` | `SORT_KEY_CANDIDATES` gains `status`, `type`, `assignee` |
| `src/cli/mod.rs:1260` | `--sort` help text documents the grammar |
| `src/cli/commands/list.rs:627` | delete `validate_sort_key`; parse to `SortSpec` in `build_filters` |
| `src/cli/commands/search.rs:501` | delete the duplicate `validate_sort_key` |
| `src/cli/commands/search.rs:618` | `apply_sort_by_issue` delegates to `SortSpec::cmp` |
| `src/storage/sqlite.rs:4053` | `ORDER BY` block collapses to `spec.order_by_sql(...)` |
| `src/storage/sqlite.rs:4811` | same, for the search builder |
| `src/storage/sqlite.rs:4352` | guard compares `resolved(reverse)` against the `updated_at ASC` ordering |
| `src/storage/sqlite.rs:10151` | `ListFilters.sort` type change, plus its test literals |
| `docs/CLI_REFERENCE.md:233` | document the grammar |

### The fast-path hazard

`list_stale_issues_for_command_output` guards an index-backed fast path at
`sqlite.rs:4352` with `filters.sort.as_deref() != Some("updated_at")`
**and** `!filters.reverse` — so it fires only when the effective ordering is
`updated_at ASC` (oldest first, which is what a stale listing wants). A
field-only replacement predicate would therefore be wrong in two directions
at once: it would fire for `updated,priority`, and it would ignore the
direction the guard actually depends on.

The correct replacement compares the resolved ordering:

```rust
filters.sort.as_ref().map(|s| s.resolved(filters.reverse))
    != Some(vec![SortKey::asc(SortField::UpdatedAt), SortKey::id_terminator()])
```

Get this wrong and the fast path returns rows in the wrong order with
nothing failing. The comparable guards at `:4223`, `:10352`, `:10373` and
`list.rs:515` only test `is_none()` and are safe as they stand, but each
must be re-read during implementation.

## Out of scope

`br ready --sort` keeps its own closed `ReadySortPolicy` enum
(`hybrid | priority | oldest`). It is a scheduling heuristic rather than a
column ordering, and merging the two concepts is not part of this work.

## Testing

Three layers, in the structure CLAUDE.md prescribes.

**Parser unit tests** in `src/model/sort.rs`: aliases, `-` and `+` prefixes,
duplicate fields, empty segments, leading and trailing commas, unknown
fields, the single-`priority` carve-out, and `--reverse` composition.

**Engine-agreement property test** in `tests/proptest/`, added to
`tests/proptest.rs` with a `#[path]` line. Generates random issue sets and
random specs, then asserts the SQL ordering and the Rust comparator produce
the same sequence. This is the invariant the whole design exists to protect
and the one failure nobody would catch by reading. Note that
`.proptest-regressions` is keyed to the source path and fails silently if the
file later moves.

**End-to-end tests** in `tests/e2e/`: the new CLI surface on `list` and
`search`, the rejection messages, and `--sort priority` output staying
byte-identical to today.

## Acceptance criteria

- `--sort` on `br list` and `br search` accepts a comma-separated spec over
  `priority`, `status`, `type`, `assignee`, `created_at`, `updated_at`,
  `title`, with `created`/`updated` aliases and `-`/`+` direction prefixes.
- A bare field uses the natural direction in the table above; `--reverse`
  flips every key; every spec ends with an implicit `id ASC`.
- `--sort priority` alone still emits `priority ASC, created_at DESC, id ASC`,
  and the no-`--sort` default is unchanged.
- `status` and `type` sort in the documented enum order, not alphabetically;
  custom values sort last and alphabetically among themselves.
- Unassigned issues sort last under both `assignee` and `-assignee`.
- Unknown fields, duplicate fields and empty segments are rejected before any
  query runs.
- The SQL and in-memory orderings agree, asserted by property test.
- The `sqlite.rs:4352` fast path fires only when the resolved ordering is
  `updated_at ASC`, never for a multi-key spec beginning with `updated_at`.
- `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN task check` exits 0.

# Global Constraints

Every task's requirements implicitly include this section. Values are copied
verbatim from `CLAUDE.md`.

## The gate — AMENDED for this epic

CLAUDE.md requires `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN task check` before **every**
commit. **The project owner has explicitly relaxed that for this epic**,
because a full gate runs clippy over every target plus all 3162 tests and
would dominate the work if run nine times.

| Task | Gate |
| --- | --- |
| Every task | `task format` + `cargo clippy --all-targets`, plus that task's own targeted `task test:one` |
| Tasks 4, 6 and 9 | **Full `task check`** — these are the checkpoints |

**`--all-targets`, not `--lib`.** The light gate originally ran `cargo clippy
--lib`, which does not lint test targets. A `needless_pass_by_value` error in a
new test helper therefore went undetected until checkpoint 2, where it failed
the gate as drift from an already-closed task. `--all-targets` is slower but
catches it at the task that introduced it.

Do not substitute your own judgement here: run exactly the gate your task
body specifies. If a checkpoint gate fails on drift introduced by an earlier
task, report it — do not silently fix another task's code.

The full gate runs `toolchain:check`, `format:check`, `lint` (clippy over
every target), then `test` (full suite, no-fail-fast).

**Always prefix `cargo`/`rustc`/`task` with `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN`.** There
is no `rust-toolchain.toml`; a stale exported `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN` silently runs
the build on nightly and still reports success.

`task test` runs cargo-nextest **and then** the doctests
(`cargo test --workspace --doc`). Both halves matter. Do not substitute a bare
`cargo nextest run`.

Run a subset with `env -u RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN task test:one -- -E 'test(<name>)'`.
Nextest selects by filterset, not `--test <binary> <name>`.

## Commits

Commit messages must parse as Conventional Commits. Accepted types: `feat`,
`fix`, `docs`, `chore`, `build`, `ci`, `test`, `perf`, `style`, `refactor`,
`revert`, plus a `!` breaking marker. **`plan:` and `spec:` are rejected** —
use `chore(...)` for bookkeeping commits.

**Never add AI or agent attribution trailers** — no `Co-Authored-By` naming an
assistant, no `Generated with …`, no variant, in any commit, PR body, tag or
release note. Strip one if a tool adds it.

Do not skip hooks. Do not pass `--no-verify`.

## Test placement

Tests live in grouped binaries, each a crate root listing `#[path]` modules
from a directory beside it:

tests/storage.rs    tests/storage/*.rs  SQLite, the JSONL mirror, sync

This epic is being implemented **directly on `main`**, at the project owner's

can be reverted cleanly. Do not create branches, do not rebase, and do not
rewrite any commit that is not your own task's.

    items: &mut [T],
    sort: Option<&SortSpec>,
    reverse: bool,
    mut issue_of: impl FnMut(&T) -> &crate::model::Issue,
) -> Result<()> {
    let default_spec;

        Some(spec) => spec,
        None => {

            &default_spec

| `type` | ascending — task, bug, feature, epic, chore, docs, question, then custom |
| `assignee` | ascending — A-Z, unassigned always last |
| `title` | ascending — A-Z, case-insensitive |
| `created_at` (`created`) | descending — newest first |
| `updated_at` (`updated`) | descending — newest first |

`-` forces descending and `+` forces ascending. `--reverse` flips every key.
Every sort ends with an implicit `id` tiebreaker, so output is deterministic.

```sh
br list --sort priority,updated     # critical first, most recent within each band
br list --sort status,priority      # group by workflow state, then priority
br list --sort -updated             # oldest first
```

`--sort priority` on its own keeps its historical tiebreaker and is
equivalent to `--sort priority,created`.
